note: Establish the valuable C5/C6 blend backbone first, leaving light and heavy tails unsold until their recovery economics are clear.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 test the high-value C5/C6 backbone: root C4/C5 split, C5/C6 split, then C6 paraffin/naphthene/heavy splits. Step 2 tune purity/cost and add heavy-product or C4 recovery only if profitable. Initial 5-column design sells C5, C6 paraffin and C6 naphthene blends, avoiding difficult pure-product polishing. Moderate stages/reflux because costs are high.

note: Replace the unprofitable blend tree with a compact heavy-end train targeting pure heptane, octane, and nonane.
notebook: PLAN: Step 1 test a low-column-count heavy-products backbone: root C6/C7 split, then heptane/octane/nonane separations. Step 2 tune heavy purity/cost. Step 3 add C5/C6 or light recovery only where incremental revenue exceeds cost. The initial C5/C6 blend tree sold nothing and cost $460M/yr, so it was abandoned. Heavy cuts have wide boiling gaps and three valuable products ($332M/$359M/$104M per year), making them a better first target.

note: Rebuild around the two most valuable blend products, C5 and C6 paraffins, with sharper root and downstream splits.
notebook: PLAN: Build a high-value blend backbone: root C5/C6 split, light removal to sell C5 mix, and C6-paraffin/heavy split. Then tune recovery/purity and add heavy products only if profitable. Current step: establish all three splits and inspect compositions. Previous heavy-only train sold nothing; C5 and C6-paraffin blends are worth roughly $0.62B and $1.15B/yr, far more attractive than small light cuts. Boil-up at the root must be high enough to keep pentanes out of the heavy stream.

note: Sharpen both downstream splits: the current C5 stream is contaminated by butane and the C6 blend by pentane, while both blends are valuable enough to justify more separation.
notebook: PLAN: Build a high-value blend backbone: root C5/C6 split, light removal to sell C5 mix, and C6-paraffin/heavy split. Then tune recovery/purity and add heavy products only if profitable. Current step: sharpen the C4/C5 and C5/C6 splits enough to reach 95% blend purity. Root split is appropriate: tops contain essentially all C5 and lights, bottoms C6+. T at 50 stages/R=B=3 left 31% butane in C5; B at 70/5/4 left 17% pentane in C6. Increase both secondary columns to 80 stages and R=B=6. C5 blend potential ~$0.62B/yr and C6 paraffin blend ~$1.1B/yr, so purity is worth substantial extra duty.

note: Increase both stage count and boil-up on the leaky splits: C5 is being lost to the root bottoms, while butane contaminates the C5 product and pentane contaminates the C6 blend.
notebook: PLAN: Establish the C5 and C6-paraffin blend backbone, then reduce duties once both products meet 95%; add other products only if marginal value exceeds cost. Step 1: intensify all three cuts, especially reboil, because the root leaks C5 downward and the C4/C5 column leaks butane downward. Current root/T/B at 70/4/5, 80/6/6, 80/6/6 gave zero sales: TB only 71% C5 and BT 80% C6 paraffins. C5 blend potential ~$479M/yr at current recovery and C6 blend ~$958M/yr, so sharpness can pay. Try 100/6/10 root, 120/6/10 T, 100/6/8 B, all dp .15. Avoid further columns until positive revenue.

note: Prune the unsold heavy branch and make the two-column C5 business much leaner, with high reboil in the C4/C5 split to stop isopentane leaking overhead.
notebook: PLAN: First obtain positive cash flow from the C5 blend using only two moderately sized columns; then restore a lean C6-paraffin branch if its marginal revenue beats cost. Step 1: root splits C5 from C6 and T removes C4 overhead. The 100-120 stage, dp=.15 design was far too costly ($916M) and still off-spec. Use root 65/4/7 dp=.05 and T 75/5/12 dp=.05; prune B. High T boil-up should retain isopentane in TB; moderate stages/duty should cut cost. Root C5 potential ~$500M/yr, so two lean columns can be profitable. Avoid C6 until C5 actually sells.

note: Reverse the split order and use moderate pressures for robust convergence: take C4 and lighter overhead at the root, then recover the C5 blend overhead from the heavy stream with leaner columns.
notebook: PLAN: Obtain positive cash flow from the C5 blend using two moderately sized columns, then add C6 only if marginal economics justify it. Step 1 now reverses the separation order: root splits C4 from C5, and B splits C5 overhead from C6+ bottoms. R45 showed the old order leaves 16% DMB in the C5 stream, so it cannot sell regardless of modest tuning. Its two columns cost $787M/yr, above C5 revenue (~$609M/yr), so use much leaner 50/4/4 and 60/6/6 settings. Moderate pressure drops (.30/.15) also avoid the high-pressure convergence failures at dp=.05-.10. Prune all other products until the C5 blend actually meets 95%.

note: The two-column attempt cannot monetize its 76%-pure C6 stream. Add the C6/C7 split and use strong reboil throughout to keep C5 out of the root tops and C6 out of the C5 product.
notebook: PLAN: Build a three-column blend train: root C4-/C5+, B C5/C6+, BB C6/C7+. Sell only the C5 and C6 paraffin blends; their combined value (~$1.54B/yr) can support three columns, unlike C5 alone. Current step tests 60 stages with strong reboil (root 10, downstream 8) to keep heavy key components in bottoms and moderate pressure drops (.5/.4/.3) for convergence. Prior two-column run split C5 almost evenly at the root, leaving only 20% C5 in BT and 76% C6; C6 therefore needs its own split. Avoid low-pressure settings that failed for agent-5. If products meet 95%, tune costs downward and only then consider heavy pure products.

note: The root and B splits are already clean; BT needs a paraffin/naphthene separation. Add that column to monetize both valuable C6 blends before addressing the light overhead.
notebook: PLAN: First monetize the clean C6+ train by splitting C6 paraffins from C6 naphthenes at BT; then add a C4/C5 split only if its value exceeds cost. Root currently sends essentially all C5 and lighter to T and C6+ to B; B cleanly separates C6 from C7+. BT is 74% C6 paraffin and 26% naphthenes, so it needs a paraffin/naphthene split, not more C7 removal. Potential C6 paraffin revenue ~$738M/yr plus naphthene blend ~$400M/yr. Current costs are excessive (root $568M, B $264M), so after purity is achieved reduce stages/reflux/boil-up. Avoid full-pressure root, which repeatedly fails for agent-5.

note: Combine the proven profitable C4/C5 train with the C6 paraffin train, using a moderately high-boilup root to prevent pentane contamination of the C6 product.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a five-column core selling n-butane, C5 blend and C6 paraffin blend; use R65's proven lean light-end settings, retain a high-boilup root for a clean C5/C6 cut, then trim costs and consider naphthenes/heavies. This is step 1 of that combined design.
R65 proves 50/2.5/2.3 root +45-stage T/TB makes $496M at $362M cost (reward .306). My old root at 60/6/10 cleanly sent C5- overhead and C6+ below, while B and BT made a sellable C6 paraffin stream. R65's root cannot directly feed the C6 train because its bottoms retain ~12% pentane. Therefore use root 50/3/6 to shift C5 upward without old extreme traffic. Keep old BT 60/6/8 initially; B eased to 50/4/4. Naphthene bottoms and C7+ remain unsold. Next inspect actual purities/costs, then reduce BT duty/stages or improve naphthene recovery only if economical.

note: Copy the proven profitable light-end core, but use an intermediate root boil-up and attach the demonstrated C6 paraffin train; this targets all three valuable products without the excessive six-column cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a five-column core selling n-butane, C5 blend and C6 paraffin blend; use R65's proven lean light-end settings, use an intermediate-boilup root for a clean C5/C6 cut, then trim costs and consider naphthenes/heavies. This is step 2 of that combined design.
R65 proves 50/2.5/2.3 root +45-stage T/TB makes $496M at $362M cost (reward .306). My old root at 60/6/10 cleanly sent C5- overhead and C6+ below, while B and BT made a sellable C6 paraffin stream. Root boilup 6 was excessive: DMB/2MP leaked overhead and TB no longer made specification products. Try root 50/3/4 as the compromise. Keep old B 50/4/4 and BT 60/6/8 initially. Naphthene bottoms and C7+ remain unsold. Next inspect purities/costs, then tune only the limiting split and reduce BT duty if possible.

note: Restore the proven low-duty root and butane/C5 products, then test whether the previously successful C6 paraffin train adds enough value to cover its cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore R93's proven profitable butane/C5 core, then attach the C6 paraffin train that already produced a $586M blend; tune or prune only based on measured marginal economics. Step: test the combined five-column design.
R93 earns $496M at $362M cost (reward .306). My current B/BT train earns $586M but costs $338M, so it could add about $249M/yr if its purity survives the restored root. Current root boilup 4 was harmful: it cost $273M and contaminated the C5 train. Restore 50/2.5/2.3. Keep B 50/4/4 dp.4 and BT 60/6/8 dp.2. Next check C6 blend recovery/purity; if profitable, reduce BT duty/stages or sell BTB only if useful. Heavies and C3/C4 tops remain unsold.

note: Reduce the dominant heavy-train stages and duties while holding all profitable light-end settings fixed; retain the design only if C6 blend purity and recovery remain adequate.
notebook:
PLAN: Keep the proven five-column butane/C5/C6 business and now reduce the two heavy-train columns' capital and energy while watching the 95% C6 blend threshold. Step: first aggressive-but-moderate cost reduction.
Current best .694: revenue 1043.7, cost 739.3. Light core is fixed and profitable. B+BT cost 377.4 and earn 547.6, so marginal profit 170.2. BTT contains much DMB but recovering it needs sharper separation; first test B 35/3/3 and BT 45/5/6. If purity survives, iterate duties/stages downward; if not, restore one setting at a time. Avoid root changes: boilup 3.5 destroyed the C5 split, while 2.3 works. Heavies and C3 tops have poor economics.

note: Restore the original high-purity C6 splitter while retaining the cheaper 35-stage B column; this isolates which reduction destroyed blend purity.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the 0.694 baseline, isolate whether the cheaper B column is compatible with the original high-purity BT split, then cautiously trim one column at a time. Step: test B=35/3/3 with BT restored to 60/6/8.
Best .694: revenue 1043.7, cost 739.3. Root 50/2.5/2.3, T45/3.5/2.5, TB45/6/5 are a reliable light core. Simultaneously cutting B and BT dropped C6 blend to 92%; most degradation likely came from BT 45/5/6. B cost fell 49.4M and its outlet composition changed only modestly, so it may be a real saving. Never use root boilup 3.5; it destroys C5 recovery. Avoid C3/heavy product expansions. If this works, test mild BT reductions, then mild root/T/TB stage cuts.

note: Adopt the proven 1.089 design: the added BTT column earns a valuable C5 blend for only $55M/yr while preserving the C6 paraffin product.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt the proven 1.089 six-column plant, then improve the marginal BTT splitter and/or reduce upstream costs without losing the three blend qualifications. Step: restore R133 exactly.
R133 adds BTT 50/4/4/0.2: its overhead is 97% C5 and earns 228.4M, while BTB remains a 95%+ C6 blend worth 547.6M. Added cost is only 55M, so this is clearly worthwhile. The failed B=35 experiment caused BTB to fall to 91% paraffins; do not repeat it. Light core root 50/2.5/2.3, T45/3.5/2.5, TB45/6/5 is reliable. Next try tuning BTT to recover more DMB overhead while retaining C5 purity, since BTTB currently has no value.

note: Adopt the proven intensified BTT splitter, which qualifies both its C5 overhead and C6-paraffin bottoms and raises reward to 1.840.
notebook:

R143 shows BTT 55/6/7/0.2 lifts reward to 1.840: both BTTT (C5, $250M) and BTTB (C6 paraffin, $339M) qualify. Added $31M duty buys $371M extra revenue. Preserve the reliable core root 50/2.5/2.3, T45/3.5/2.5, TB45/6/5 and B/BT settings. Failed B=35 destroyed BTB purity, so avoid upstream cuts unless carefully tested. Next consider modest BTT tuning around 55/6/7 and potentially monetizing TT.

R152 proves BT 55/5.5/7 replaces 60/6/8, saves $16.5M net and increases revenue $9.1M: reward 1.904. All other settings unchanged. Core products: butane 96%, C5 blends TBB/BTTT, C6 blends BTB/BTTB. Avoid B-stage cuts, which previously destroyed BTB. Remaining likely tests: modest BTT duty reduction or further BT trimming, one variable at a time.

note: Copy the proven 1.937 plant and modestly reduce BTT stages and duties; both product blends currently have enough purity margin to test this saving.
notebook:

R159's BT 50/5.5/6.5 improves revenue and cuts cost versus R152. Its BTTT is 84% N-pentane +16% isopentane and BTTB is ~98% C6 paraffins, so both have modest purity margin. Test BTT 50/5.5/6.5 to reduce its $81M/yr cost. Avoid B-stage cuts, which previously destroyed BTB qualification. Current core: butane, two C5 blends, two C6-paraffin blends; TT and BB remain unsold and are not worth new columns with five solves left.

note: Trim only BTT from 50 to 45 stages, holding its successful reflux and boil-up fixed; both product blends currently have some purity margin and the best valid design is protected.
notebook:

R167 shows BT 45/6.0 destroys BTTB, so leave BT at 50/5.5/6.5. TT and BB remain unsold and are not worth new columns. Best valid design is retained if this test regresses.

notebook:
PLAN: Restore the best 50-stage BTT geometry and make one final energy-only trim; retain the best valid plant afterward. Step: test BTT reflux 5.0 versus 5.5, then stop unless the result clearly supports one last safe adjustment.
Best valid is 1.947 with BTT 50/5.5/6.5. BTT at 45 stages reduced revenue more than cost, so stage trimming is unhelpful. Both BTT products qualify comfortably as blends: BTTT is 99% C5 and BTTB about 98-99% C6 paraffins. A modest reflux trim may cut duty while retaining qualification. R167 proves BT 45/6.0 destroys BTTB, so leave BT fixed. TT and BB are not worth extra columns. R175's B-stage trim also regressed.

note: Adopt the fully simulated 1.956 plant: its modest BTT boil-up reduction improves both revenue and cost relative to the current design.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt the best proven valid configuration with the final evaluation, then stop. Step: copy R182, whose BTT duty trim improves both reward and revenue over my best, and make no further changes.
R182 scores 1.956 with root 50/2.5/2.3/0.5; B 50/4/4/0.4; T 45/3.5/2.5/0.3; BT 50/5.5/6.5/0.2; TB 45/6/5/0.3; BTT 50/5/6/0.2. It improves on my 1.947 baseline by reducing BTT duties while both blend products still qualify. Stage cuts and BT changes were harmful, and TT/BB do not justify added columns.
